# Installation

[← README](../README.md) · [Usage](USAGE.md)

You need Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Python 3.10, and the CUDA 12.4 development toolkit. The tested environment uses PyTorch 2.4.0, torchvision 0.19.0, and cutoop 0.1.0.

## 1. Create the environment

Run these commands from the repository root:

```bash
python3.10 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-lock-cu124.txt
```

The lock file contains the tested dependencies, including Gradio and SAM. `requirements-cu124.txt` lists the main dependencies if you maintain your own environment.

## 2. Build the CUDA extensions

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.4
export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST='8.9'  # RTX 4090; use '9.0' for H200
export MAX_JOBS=4

python -m pip install --no-build-isolation --no-deps \
  ./third_party/pointnet2_ops ./third_party/chamfer
python -m pip install -e '.[demo,test]'
```

Set `CUDA_HOME` to your toolkit location and choose the architecture for your GPU. Rebuild both extensions after changing PyTorch, CUDA, or GPU architecture; remove their generated `build/` directories first.

To check the installation:

```bash
python -m pytest tests -q
python -m pip check
f2g-pose --help
```

## 3. Set up RADIO

F2G-Pose uses **RADIO v2.5-L**, with features from layers 8, 16, and 23. Install this pinned source revision:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/NVlabs/RADIO.git third_party_local/RADIO
git -C third_party_local/RADIO checkout fbd19ec1e68483482d7d96a59cb639880a8b33ed

export F2G_RADIO_REPOSITORY="$PWD/third_party_local/RADIO"
export F2G_RADIO_CHECKPOINT="$PWD/weights/radio-v2.5-l_half.pth.tar"

python scripts/download_weights.py \
  --url 'https://huggingface.co/nvidia/RADIO/resolve/main/radio-v2.5-l_half.pth.tar?download=true' \
  --sha256 50324e8cb086885126a896ad9ecbac46355cf0e4c1d8363763b01693a4618ff1 \
  --output weights/radio-v2.5-l_half.pth.tar
```

Set the two `F2G_RADIO_*` variables in each new shell, or pass `--radio-repository` and `--radio-checkpoint` to the CLI. RADIO has its own [NVIDIA license and model card](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/RADIO).

## 4. Add the F2G-Pose weights

Download the [F2G-Pose checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/J3rr1/F2G-Pose) and verify its SHA-256:

```bash
python scripts/download_weights.py \
  --url 'https://huggingface.co/J3rr1/F2G-Pose/resolve/main/f2g-pose.pt?download=true' \
  --sha256 bff06bd58a42fd805d8232f9ab7b4612b8eb833edf6b6cccd23e5040a8c9ca18 \
  --output weights/f2g-pose.pt
```

If you downloaded the complete weight package, run `sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS` from that directory before copying `f2g-pose.pt` to `weights/`.

The model configuration is included in the checkpoint. You are ready to [launch the demo or run inference](USAGE.md).

## Optional: SAM object selection

To select an object with clicks or a box instead of uploading a mask, download the official [SAM ViT-B](https://github.com/facebookresearch/segment-anything) checkpoint:

```bash
python scripts/download_weights.py \
  --url https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/segment_anything/sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth \
  --sha256 ec2df62732614e57411cdcf32a23ffdf28910380d03139ee0f4fcbe91eb8c912 \
  --output weights/sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth
```

Pass `--sam-checkpoint weights/sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth` when starting the demo.

# Deployment

[← README](../README.md) · [Installation](INSTALL.md) · [Local demo](USAGE.md#interactive-demo)

The local NVIDIA GPU demo is tested. The Dockerfile and ZeroGPU app are provided for deployment; container execution and hosted ZeroGPU still need validation on the target service.

## Docker

Place `f2g-pose.pt` and `radio-v2.5-l_half.pth.tar` in `weights/`, then build and run:

```bash
docker build --build-arg TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.9 -t f2g-pose:local .
docker run --rm --gpus all -p 127.0.0.1:7860:7860 \
  -v "$PWD/weights:/weights:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/demo_outputs:/outputs" f2g-pose:local
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:7860. Use architecture `8.9` for RTX 4090 or `9.0` for H200. The image includes the pinned RADIO source; weights are loaded from the mounted directory.

To enable SAM, add `sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth` to `weights/` and run:

```bash
docker run --rm --gpus all -p 127.0.0.1:7860:7860 \
  -v "$PWD/weights:/weights:ro" \
  -v "$PWD/demo_outputs:/outputs" f2g-pose:local \
  f2g-pose demo --checkpoint /weights/f2g-pose.pt \
  --sam-checkpoint /weights/sam_vit_b_01ec64.pth \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 7860 --output-root /outputs
```

## Hugging Face Docker Space

Use the same Dockerfile with the Docker SDK and app port **7860**. Provide an NVIDIA GPU, mount or download the weights, and configure `F2G_RADIO_CHECKPOINT` and the demo checkpoint path for your storage location.

## Hugging Face ZeroGPU

`deploy/zerogpu_app.py` uses the same Gradio interface and creates the model inside a `@spaces.GPU` callback. Use a separate environment from the PyTorch 2.4 reference installation:

```bash
python -m pip install -r deploy/zerogpu-requirements.txt
python -m pip install --no-build-isolation --no-deps \
  ./third_party/pointnet2_ops ./third_party/chamfer
python -m pip install --no-build-isolation --no-deps .
```

The deployment requirements pin PyTorch 2.8. Build the extensions with a CUDA toolkit and architecture compatible with the assigned GPU; the [ZeroGPU documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-zerogpu) describes the hosted runtime.

Set these environment variables:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `F2G_CHECKPOINT` | Path to `f2g-pose.pt` |
| `F2G_RADIO_REPOSITORY` | Path to the pinned RADIO checkout |
| `F2G_RADIO_CHECKPOINT` | Path to the RADIO v2.5-L weight file |
| `F2G_SAM_CHECKPOINT` | Optional SAM ViT-B checkpoint |
| `F2G_OUTPUT_ROOT` | Optional output directory; default `demo_outputs` |

Copy the metadata from [deploy/README.space.md](../deploy/README.space.md) into the Space's root README. The app loads F2G-Pose per GPU allocation. `deploy/probe_zerogpu.py` provides a local compatibility check; PyTorch 2.8 / CUDA 12.8 checks have passed on RTX 4090, while the hosted allocation path remains untested.

Policy-Mask: Budget-Aware Adaptation of Diffusion Features to Discriminative Tasks

Ivan Listopadov    Maksim Nakhodnov    Aibek Alanov Affiliation: HSE University Affiliation: MSU Affiliation: Constructor University Affiliation: FusionBrain Lab, AXXX
Abstract

Selecting intermediate features from a frozen diffusion model for discriminative tasks is non-trivial because the useful signal is distributed across the denoising trajectory, network depth, and channels. In practice, this requires choosing a timestep, a block, and a channel subset. Existing methods either fix these choices by hand or optimize only a few extraction hyperparameters, most often the timestep, then reuse the same rule across inputs and budgets. We introduce Policy-Mask, a budget-conditioned policy trained on the downstream objective that jointly selects all three under a prescribed channel budget. Without normalization, the channel-score contribution grows with the number of selected channels and dominates the timestep and block updates. We normalize it by subset cardinality, keeping the three policy heads on comparable scales and stabilizing joint training. At matched budgets, Policy-Mask improves over fixed extraction and feature-filter baselines across segmentation, classification, and semantic correspondence, reaching 38.9 mIoU on ADE20K, 75.4% top-1 on CIFAR-100 at 128 dimensions, and 76.3 PCK@0.1 on SPair-71k. Component-wise ablations show that block selection materially affects downstream accuracy, and the highest recorded channel-budget score occurs at 256 retained channels, identifying a practical operating point for compact diffusion representations. We further adapt Policy-Mask to diffusion transformers, including PixArt-Σ\Sigma and SD3.5 MMDiT, by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models learn intermediate representations that support semantic segmentation, image classification, and semantic correspondence (Baranchuk et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023). Using these representations for a downstream task requires choosing which activations to extract. The available features depend on the denoising timestep and network layer, and each feature map contains a set of channels from which the task representation is formed.

Existing methods address this choice through fixed extraction rules, learned aggregation across timesteps and layers, or timestep selection during distillation (Luo et al., 2023; Yang and Wang, 2023). RepFusion transfers features from a frozen diffusion teacher to a student and learns which timestep to use. This leaves the choice of layer and retained feature dimensions as further parts of the extraction problem. These choices also determine which activations must be stored and used as distillation targets.

Policy-Mask selects a timestep, a layer, and a channel subset under a prescribed channel budget. The policy takes the input image and budget and selects an action a=(t,l,K)a=(t,l,K) with |K|=b|K|=b. A task decoder provides the selection reward, and the selected features supervise the student during training. At inference, the student processes the image without evaluating the diffusion teacher. This extends RepFusion’s timestep selection to a joint choice of extraction point and feature subset.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A budgeted (t,l,K)(t,l,K) policy with exact-cardinality sampling.

  2. 2.

    A channel-score normalization that controls the relative action-head contributions.

  3. 3.

    At 128 of 1280 aligned channels, gains of 1.2–1.6 mIoU over full-width fixed extraction on four segmentation benchmarks.

  4. 4.

    A formal action mapping from U-Net features to DiT, MMDiT, and flow transformer feature lattices.

2 Related work

Diffusion representations. Diffusion features support dense prediction, correspondence, segmentation, and depth estimation through task-specific extraction rules (Baranchuk et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2023; Yang and Wang, 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Ji et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Ke et al., 2024). Recent work studies prompt selection, noise-free representations, and the transfer of stable diffusion to dense tasks (Li et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Kondapaneni et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Stracke et al., 2025; Ravishankar et al., 2025). RepFusion is the closest predecessor: it distills a recognizer from a frozen diffusion teacher after selecting a useful noise step (Yang and Wang, 2023). Policy-Mask keeps the same teacher–student division and expands the selected object to (t,l,K)(t,l,K).

Budgeted subset selection. Feature selection spans filters, wrappers, continuous relaxations, and greedy methods (Peng et al., 2005; Kohavi and John, 1997; Abid et al., 2019; Das and Kempe, 2011; Elenberg et al., 2018; Mirzasoleiman et al., 2015; Nemhauser et al., 1978). Policy-Mask selects feature dimensions of one frozen model response. Budget-conditioned policies also appear in diffusion caching, where ReCache selects recomputation steps under an inference budget (Aliev et al., 2026). Here the budget constrains feature coordinates used for distillation. The policy uses a Plackett–Luce ordering and a Gumbel top-bb sampler (Plackett, 1975; Kool et al., 2019). Its gradient estimator follows the standard score-function construction with a baseline (Greensmith et al., 2004; Kool et al., 2020).

3.3 Channel-score normalization

The channel score in Equation 6 is a sum of bb terms, whereas the timestep and layer scores each contain one term. Dividing the channel score by bb replaces this sum with its mean and controls its relative weight in the joint update. It does not assume that gradient norms grow linearly with bb. We use:

g^bal=(R−c)​∇θ[log⁡πt+log⁡πl+1b​log⁡πσ].\widehat{g}_{\rm bal}=(R-c)\nabla_{\theta}\left[\log\pi_{t}+\log\pi_{l}+\frac{1}{b}\log\pi_{\sigma}\right]. (8)

The 1/b1/b factor is a preconditioner, so the controlled update is not claimed to be an unbiased estimator of ∇θJb\nabla_{\theta}J_{b}. For disjoint heads and plain SGD, it is equivalent to reducing only the channel-head learning rate by bb. With a shared trunk, adaptive moments, and entropy regularization, it instead changes the relative head contribution (Chen et al., 2018). The action-axis ablation motivates this control: the unnormalized joint policy reaches 31.68 mIoU, compared with 31.78 for the timestep-only policy (Figure 4). With fixed alignment, normalization raises mean best-validation mIoU from 36.8 to 37.7 over three seeds (Table 5).

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental setup

Teacher and student. The main selector comparisons use a frozen SD-1.5 U-Net and a common width of 1280 aligned channels. Compact selectors retain 128 channels. The student loss and updates are given in Equation 2 and Algorithm 1.

Datasets and metrics. Segmentation is evaluated on ADE20K (Zhou et al., 2017), Cityscapes (Cordts et al., 2016), CelebA-HQ (Karras et al., 2018), and Pascal VOC (Everingham et al., 2010) using mIoU. Classification uses CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky, 2009) top-1 accuracy. Semantic correspondence uses SPair-71k (Min et al., 2019) PCK@0.1 with image and bounding-box normalization reported separately.

Baselines. The baselines include fixed extraction, top-variance and Fisher channel selection, and full-width extraction. The DDAE (Xiang et al., 2023) and RepFusion (Yang and Wang, 2023) entries in Table 2 retain their corresponding source protocols.

4.2 Main results

At 128 selected channels, Policy-Mask exceeds full-width extraction at a fixed (t,l)(t,l) by 1.5, 1.6, 1.2, and 1.3 mIoU on ADE20K, Cityscapes, CelebA-HQ, and Pascal VOC, respectively (Table 1). These results compare feature-selection rules at 10% of the full aligned width.

At 128 dimensions, Policy-Mask reaches 95.2% top-1 on CIFAR-10 and 75.4% on CIFAR-100, 1.0 and 1.3 points above the reported RepFusion entries (Table 2). On SPair-71k, it reaches 76.3 PCK@0.1 with image normalization and 67.5 with bounding-box normalization.

Figure 3 shows corrected facade labels and fewer false regions in cemetery, bakery, and sea scenes among the outcome-selected examples. The corresponding losses and class-wise differences are reported in Appendix C.

4.3 Ablation study

Action axes. In the controlled action-axis ablation, expanding a timestep-only policy to the time–layer grid raises mIoU from 31.78 to 33.32. Adding a heuristic top-bb subset reaches 32.82, while the unnormalized joint policy reaches 31.68 (Figure 4). Expanding the action space alone therefore does not improve accuracy in this setting.

Channel-score normalization. With AlA_{l} fixed, Policy-Mask reaches 37.7±0.737.7\pm 0.7 mIoU, compared with 36.8±0.636.8\pm 0.6 without the 1/b1/b channel-score factor (Table 5). Both use the same three seeds and training settings. This comparison is separate from the single-seed action-axis ablation and the main segmentation table.

Increasing bb from 128 to 256 raises the best validation mIoU by 0.72 and the mean over the last five epochs by 0.27. The sweep changes both the selected features and the KD-loss scale, so it does not identify an optimal budget independently of distillation strength (Appendix A.1). 5 Conclusion

We presented Policy-Mask, which treats diffusion feature extraction as a budgeted decision: a policy jointly selects the timestep, the layer, and an exact-size channel subset of a frozen teacher, and the selected features distill a student that runs alone at inference. The experiments support three conclusions. First, joint selection pays off at a fixed budget: with 128 of 1280 channels, Policy-Mask exceeds full-width extraction at a fixed extraction point on all four segmentation benchmarks and exceeds RepFusion on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Second, channel-score normalization improves the tested joint policy. Without the 1/b1/b factor, the joint policy falls below the timestep-only policy in the action-axis ablation. With fixed alignment, normalization raises ADE20K mIoU from 36.8 to 37.7 over three seeds. Third, the action transfers to DiT and MMDiT teachers by replacing U-Net channels with image-token hidden dimensions while retaining the student loss and exact-cardinality constraint. Separating channel count from distillation strength remains the main open question for choosing the operating budget.

Abstract

As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70–80% of the experts, substantially improving the model’s scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

1 Introduction

In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have gradually approached or even surpassed human-level ability in general text, mathematics, and code (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI et al., 2024). This progress owes much to the increasing scale of model parameters and training data: intelligence has been improved substantially as both factors grow (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022b).

To enable ever-larger models, parameter sparsification has become an important approach (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2025). As the module that accounts for the vast majority of model parameters, the feed-forward network was originally a densely computed block. (Vaswani et al., 2017a). However, as model size grows, such dense computation gradually becomes prohibitively expensive, creating efficiency bottlenecks for both training and inference (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022). Meanwhile, although feed-forward networks are densely computed, only a sparse subset of parameters is actually activated for a given token during its forward pass (Li et al., 2023; Mirzadeh et al., 2024); the remaining inactive parameters still participate in the computation, leading to substantial waste.

To address this, researchers have proposed designing feed-forward networks with a natively sparse-activation structure, most notably the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). MoE splits the feed-forward network into multiple sub-networks along the intermediate dimension and routes each token to only a limited number of them before computation. This design endows the model with a large total parameter count while ensuring that each token’s forward pass computation uses only a small fraction of parameters, reconciling scale with efficiency.

With the advent of increasingly sparse MoE models, parameter efficiency along the width dimension has been steadily improved (Dai et al., 2024). In this work, however, we ask how parameter efficiency can be improved along the depth dimension (Raposo et al., 2024). On the one hand, interpretability studies suggest that feed-forward networks store relatively static knowledge (Geva et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022), and that different layers may store similar knowledge, suggesting nontrivial redundancy across layers (Meng et al., 2022; Takase and Kiyono, 2023; Fan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2025; Men et al., 2025). On the other hand, Looped Transformers reuse the same parameters across recurrent applications of a block (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2019; Csordás et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a),and recent work shows that this design can attain the reasoning performance of much larger models with far fewer parameters (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). This benefit, however, comes with additional recursions and greater serial depth, incurring higher computational and latency costs.

To balance parameter storage efficiency and computational cost, this work explores the potential of another Parameter Loop scheme — Cross-Layer Expert Sharing. Unlike Looped Transformers, which keep the total parameters of each layer unchanged but increase the number of recursions, we aim to keep the number of recursions unchanged while increasing the candidate experts of each layer, and use the sparse activation of MoE to keep both the activated parameters and the computation per layer unchanged. We refer to the experts shared across layers as Meta Experts, and the layer-private experts in the conventional design as Local Experts.

Our experiments show that, compared with the Local Expert of hierarchical architectures, Meta Experts reduce parameter redundancy and achieve lower cross-entropy loss together with higher downstream task accuracy. At a fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, our model achieves comparable performance to Vanilla MoE with only 70% as many experts, indicating a substantially higher effective capacity per parameter. Further analysis reveals another reason why cross-layer expert sharing is effective: Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible paths for storage and retrieval. Compared with hierarchical architectures, cross-layer expert sharing implicitly provides more flexible residual connections: beyond the forward residual connections, it introduces a backward residual connection at the activation level—one that operates within a single forward pass and is therefore absent from existing models.

Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) A systematic analysis of the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, covering their activation and total-number ratios among all experts, their presence in every layer, and their partial hierarchical organization. Although these configurations moderately affect performance, Meta Experts consistently bring significant improvements. (2) An explanation of why Meta Experts are effective from the perspective of residual connections. By comparing the forward hidden-state updates and the backward parameter updates of models with and without Meta Experts, we show that this design grants shallow and deep layers bidirectional access to representations across depth, enabling more flexible information retrieval.

3 Empirical Comparison between Meta and Local Experts

To systematically analyze the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, we start from a model with only Local Experts and incorporate Meta Experts in various forms, comparing model capabilities with and without them.

3.1 Setups

Core Variables. We consider two types of relationship between Meta Experts and Local Experts: (1) the quantitative relationship: the ratio of their total numbers within the whole model and their activated numbers within each layer (See Fig 3.(a)); (2) the topological relationship: whether every layer contains both Meta and Local Experts (See Fig 3.(b)), and whether the Meta Experts are also hierarchically organized (See Fig 3.(c)).

Common Settings. During the experiments, we first sweep all the variables on a 2B-A0.5B model, and then select the relatively better-performing configurations for the scaling ladder experiments. Throughout the experiments, we keep the total number of experts and the total activation count fixed, which indirectly ensures that different models have similar FLOPs, enabling a fairer comparison. When comparing models at different FLOPs, all models adopt the training-optimal configuration of the Vanilla MoE structure, rather than a configuration tuned specifically for our design. Detailed experimental setups can be found in A.3

Metrics. In addition to cross-entropy loss and downstream task accuracy, we introduce an expert-redundancy metric as a complementary perspective for analyzing expert specialization under different architectural settings. It allows us to examine how expert topology affects the overlap among learned expert functions. The exact training configurations and the definition of the redundancy metric are deferred to Appendix A.2.

3.2 Meta/Local Experts’ ratio

We first study the effect of the ratio between the total numbers of Meta Experts and Local Experts, and of their activation ratio within each layer, on model performance.

Settings. For the total-number ratio, we consider Meta Expert proportions of 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%; for the activation ratio, we consider proportions of 25%, 50%, or 75%. For concreteness, consider a two-layer model with 256 experts in total and 8 experts activated per layer. A Meta/Local number ratio of 75% then corresponds to 192 Meta Experts, shared across all layers, and 32 Local Experts per layer; an activation ratio of 75% corresponds to activating 6 Meta Experts and 2 Local Experts per layer.

Pilot Experiments (Fig 4). The results show that, at any activation ratio, a higher total-parameter proportion of Meta Experts consistently leads to lower loss and redundancy; meanwhile, allocating a higher activation ratio to Meta Experts also helps reduce the loss. Taken together, these observations attest to the effectiveness of Meta Experts. On the other hand, while assigning a higher activation ratio to Local Experts is detrimental to the loss, it does help reduce the redundancy among experts. This suggests that, compared with Meta Experts, Local Experts—each of which is activated in only one layer under the traditional architecture—may be harder to train sufficiently, and this under-training may give rise to redundancy.

Scaling Ladder (Fig 5). Given that activating 4 Meta Experts and 4 Local Experts per layer yields consistently better loss, we hold this activation ratio fixed and conduct a full scaling-ladder validation across the total-number ratios of 25%/50%/75%. The results confirm that, although still slightly worse than the Pure-Meta-Expert setting, the 75%75\% ratio achieves the best performance over all Partial-Meta settings at every compute budget, in terms of both cross-entropy loss and expert redundancy. Considering that a model with only Meta Experts may suffer from training instability, we adopt the 75% configuration in all subsequent experiments.

3.3 Meta/Local Experts’ topology

We next investigate the effect of the topology of Meta/Local Experts on model performance. On the one hand, we explore whether every layer should include Meta Experts; on the other hand, we explore whether the Meta Experts should themselves be partially hierarchically organized.

Settings. On the one hand, we consider variants in which Local Experts are used exclusively, with no Meta Experts introduced at all: either in only the first 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers of the model, in only the last 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers, or in both the first and the last 1, 2, or 4 layers. On the other hand, we consider partitioning the Meta Experts into 2, 4, or 8 sub-pools, which are then accessed in a looped manner—either in a chunked or an interleaved fashion.

Pilot Experiments (Fig 6). It can be observed that both operations—introducing Local-Experts-only layers, and organizing the Meta Experts hierarchically so as to mimic the topology of Local Experts—generally incur a loss degradation, which further demonstrates the positive role of Meta Experts in model performance. Notably, under a lighter degree of intervention, the loss slightly improves: for example, when only the first two and the last two layers are restricted to Local Experts, or when the Meta Experts are looped only twice. This suggests, on the one hand, that experts in the shallowest and deepest layers serve more differentiated functions, with essentially no mutual redundancy between these layers—a conclusion also supported by the expert redundancy measurements. On the other hand, mildly hierarchical Meta Experts help improve the model capability slightly; hierarchy, however, introduces a certain amount of expert redundancy, and why this redundancy does not translate into a higher loss remains an open question for further investigation.

Scaling Ladder (Fig 7). Compared with other configurations, introducing Local-Experts-only layers at both the shallow and the deep ends, and partitioning the Meta Experts into sub-pools in an interleaved manner, yield consistently better results; we therefore supplement full scaling-ladder validation under these two configurations. The results show that, at every FLOPs configuration, the best performance is achieved by using Local Experts exclusively in the first two and the last two layers, together with partitioning the Meta Experts into 2 sub-pools. We also observe that, as the model becomes deeper, using more Local-Experts-only layers and a larger hierarchy of Meta Experts likewise exhibits better results. This suggests, on the one hand, that the proportion of specialized shallow and deep layers relative to the total number of layers may remain roughly constant as model depth changes; on the other hand, deeper models also call for a larger hierarchical expert topology; the Local Experts of the Vanilla model, however, are overly hierarchical, and can therefore only achieve suboptimal results.

Overall Comparison (Fig 1 & 8) We combine the best configurations identified in each ablation and find that the combined model consistently outperforms every individual configuration in terms of loss. Building on this best configuration, we further reduce the number of Meta Experts and find that, compared with the Vanilla model, models with Meta Experts save approximately 20–30% of the experts (or 15–25% of the parameters, since other modules also account for a certain fraction of the parameters), with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the model size grows.

3.4 Downstream Performance of Meta Experts-based Model

For a more comprehensive comparison, beyond cross-entropy loss, we further compare the downstream task capabilities of different configurations through training at a larger scale.

Settings. Using the best configuration identified in each of the ablation studies above, we train 6B-A1.6B models for 200B tokens and evaluate their downstream task performance. We compare five variants: the Vanilla baseline (Vanilla MoE, Local Experts only), the MR75 model, which activates Meta Experts at a 75% meta ratio, and three topological refinements of MR75—MR75 + Loop2, which partitions the Meta Experts into two interleaved sub-pools; MR75 + F2L2, which restricts the first two and last two layers to Local Experts only; and their combination, MR75 + F2L2 + Loop2. All variants use the same total number of experts, per-layer activation budget, and training recipe, ensuring that performance differences are attributable to the expert topology. We evaluate the models across a diverse set of benchmarks covering complementary capabilities: world knowledge and factual question answering in both English (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021)) and Chinese (C-Eval (Huang et al., 2023) and CMMLU (Li et al., 2024)); multi-step and commonsense reasoning (BBH (Kazemi et al., 2025) with chain-of-thought and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018)); and open-ended, knowledge-intensive generation (TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017)).

5 Conclusion

In this work, we present an empirical and theoretical analysis of cross-layer expert sharing in MoE models, contrasting the hierarchically arranged Local Experts of standard architectures with inter-layer shared Meta Experts. Our systematic comparisons—over the Meta/Local ratio, the activation ratio, and the topology of the shared pool—show that Meta Experts consistently reduce expert redundancy and cross-entropy loss while improving downstream task accuracy: at a fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, models built on shared experts match the performance of Vanilla MoE with only 70–80% of the expert budget, substantially improving scaling potential. Beyond these empirical observations, our analysis shows that a shared expert block is not merely a parameter-saving device: it widens the forward residual connections and grants hidden states bidirectional access to expert content across depth, improving both the storage and the retrieval of information. Taken together, our results suggest that inter-layer redundancy, long treated as an intrinsic cost of deep MoE models, can instead be converted into effective capacity. Future directions include extending this analysis to larger models and broader architectures, and understanding why mildly hierarchical shared experts introduce redundancy without degrading performance.

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Related Work

Weight Tying was originally introduced to share parameters between the embedding layer and the language model head (Press and Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2016): since the two matrices map tokens to and from the hidden space, tying them nearly halves the corresponding parameters while often improving perplexity, and the practice has become standard in modern language models (Vaswani et al., 2017b; Raffel et al., 2020). Beyond tying modules at the same depth, weight tying can be pushed further, to reusing parameters across depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019).

Looped Transformer pushes weight tying to extreme: the same block is applied multiple times per token, unrolling a small set of weights into arbitrary depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Hua et al., 2025). This line of work shows that weight reuse across depth can substitute for parameter growth, and that a compact recurrent model can match the reasoning performance of much larger ones (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), at the cost of additional recursions and a higher degree of serialization. Meta Experts share the same motivation—extracting more effective capacity from a fixed parameter budget—but apply tying at a finer granularity and within a single feed-forward pass: only the expert block is reused across layers, without extra recursions, so training and inference retain the parallelism of standard Transformers, while attention may remain layer-specific. Depending on what is reused across depth, this paradigm subsumes several lines of work.

Attn Weight Sharing reuses the attention projections (or entire attention blocks) of different layers, yielding moderate parameter savings at little accuracy cost (Xiao et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2026). These results suggest that the per-layer parameter budget of Transformers is partially redundant—but leave open where the redundancy concentrates and whether the same principle applies to the rest of the block. Attn KV-Cache Sharing reuses not parameters but activations: in long-context or serving scenarios, multiple layers attend to a common KV cache, trading representational independence for inference memory and throughput (Sun et al., 2024; Brandon et al., 2024; Zuhri et al., 2025; Wu and Tu, 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Such sharing is typically applied at deployment time, affects the cache rather than the learned weights, and is often found to be nearly lossless—suggesting that layers can tolerate reading the same content, but not that they should store the same content. Meta Experts operate on the storage side: the shared expert pool is written by every layer during training, so cross-layer sharing reshapes what the model stores and how hidden states retrieve it, rather than merely reusing cached activations at inference.

FFN Weight Sharing is the closest line to our work: it reuses feed-forward parameters across layers, either by tying the FFN of all layers or by sharing it among a subset (Lan et al., 2019; Pires et al., 2023; Thawakar et al., 2024). Existing studies, however, focus on dense FFNs and report mixed results, and sharing is typically applied uniformly to every layer. MoE Weight Sharing has been explored in several recent works: experts are shared across layers, but almost always under an every-layer sharing topology, whose communication and memory overhead is difficult to scale (Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Jiao et al., 2026). Meta Experts generalize this idea to a more flexible regime: a shared pool of experts is accessed through several topology that is more friendly for communication and memory (reserving boundary layers for local experts, sub-pool partitioning with chunked or interleaved access), allows the model to decide which content is worth sharing across depth—and, as our analysis shows, implicitly turns the shared experts into bidirectional residual pathways between layers.

A.2 Redundancy Metric

To quantify how much of a model’s expert capacity is redundant, we need a measure that is (i) continuous, with no similarity threshold; (ii) comparable across architectures with different expert counts and depths; and (iii) faithful to the correlation structure among experts in high dimensions, where naive cosine similarities collapse toward zero. A.3 Scaling-ladder experimental settings

Models and training.

All models are trained from scratch on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The scaling experiments use a single family of Qwen3.5-style, text-only Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models arranged as a depth-controlled ladder at four depths L∈{12,16,20,24}L\in\{12,16,20,24\}; model width is scaled jointly with depth so that each rung is (approximately) compute-optimal, giving a clean compute-versus-loss axis. At each rung, the vanilla baseline and every Meta Experts variant are trained independently, sharing the same backbone architecture and training configuration but no trained weights, and preserving the same 128×L128\times L routed-expert budget, so only the depth-dependent knobs (width, batch size, learning rate, token budget, and expert parallelism) change across rungs (Tables 2 and 3).

Each model is a hybrid-attention MoE transformer: attention layers alternate in a fixed period-4 pattern of three gated-delta-net (GDN) linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer, so one quarter of the layers use full softmax attention—with grouped-query attention and a head dimension of 256256—while the GDN layers use a key/value head dimension of 128128 with a depthwise causal convolution of kernel width 44. Every transformer block carries an MoE feed-forward layer with 128128 routed experts and one gated shared expert, whose intermediate widths scale with model width, and the router selects the top-88 experts per token with pre-softmax gating.

We optimize with Muon (extra scale factor 0.20.2) under a warmup–stable–decay (WSD) schedule with an inverse-square-root decay shape: the peak learning rate decreases with depth (from 1.97×10−31.97\times 10^{-3} at L=12L{=}12 to 1.278×10−31.278\times 10^{-3} at L=24L{=}24), the minimum is one tenth of the peak, warmup spans tens of steps, and the decay phase spans the final ∼10%\sim\!10\% of training; all models use a micro-batch size of 22 and a sequence length of 81928192. The reported loss is the training language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten steps, so all rungs are compared on the same quantity, and the per-rung token budget is GBS×8192×iters\mathrm{GBS}\times 8192\times\text{iters} (Table 3).

All rungs use tensor-, pipeline-, and context-parallel size 11, scaling by data and expert parallelism only: the two smaller rungs (L∈{12,16}L\in\{12,16\}) use expert-parallel size 11 with the all-gather token dispatcher, and the two larger rungs (L∈{20,24}L\in\{20,24\}) use expert-parallel size 88, the all-to-all dispatcher, and block activation recomputation on the last 44 layers, with grouped GEMM and permute fusion enabled throughout. As an illustrative parameter scale, the L=16L{=}16 vanilla backbone has ≈1.96\approx\!1.96B total parameters and ≈449\approx\!449M activated parameters per token.

Hyperparameter selection.

We do not tune the training hyperparameters per architectural variant. Instead we fix a single compute-optimal configuration for the vanilla baseline backbone at each rung and reuse it unchanged for every Meta Experts variant. The baseline configuration—the joint depth–width scaling, and the per-depth global batch size, peak learning rate, and token budget—is obtained by sweeping these settings and retaining the compute-optimal choice at each depth, following established practice on compute-optimal training and its schedule (Hoffmann et al., 2022a; Hägele et al., 2024) and on scaling laws for the learning rate and batch size (Bi et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025). The Mixture-of-Experts structural choices (expert count, granularity, and the shared-expert ratio) are likewise set in line with recent MoE scaling-law analyses (Tian et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025). Because every Meta Experts variant inherits the baseline configuration without re-tuning, a difference in loss at a rung reflects the architectural change rather than a difference in hyperparameters; this reuse is further supported by evidence that optimal learning rate and batch size are governed primarily by the compute budget and are largely insensitive to Mixture-of-Experts architectural variation (Team et al., 2025). Moreover, at a given depth every variant keeps the per-token top-88 routing and hence the same activated parameters, and shares the same token budget, so all variants at a rung incur the same training FLOPs and are plotted at a single shared compute coordinate; the compute-versus-loss comparison at that rung is thus iso-FLOP by construction, and the only free axis across variants is the loss.

IQuest-Q1: Advancing Foundation Capabilities
for Agentic CLI Systems

IQuest Research
Abstract

We present IQuest-Q1, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agentic foundation model with 320B total parameters (15B activated). IQuest-Q1 is developed through a three-stage process: (1) stable and efficient pre-training, combining Stable SplitNorm, Muon, and μ\muP with a two-stage curriculum whose second stage increases the coding-data mixture, preserving a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates; (2) fine-grained mid-training, expanding the data mixture across domains and formats and progressively extending the context; and (3) multi-scaffold with multi-version post-training, combining SFT, domain-specialized RL, and MOPD across various scaffolds to integrate complementary training signals and strengthen agentic coding capabilities. Furthermore, model merging combines different experts and checkpoints from different stages while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates. The resulting IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities in both coding and general tasks. We release IQuest-Q1 as an open-source model to support community research and development.

1 Introduction

LLM-based agents allow language models [47, 5, 12, 90, 61, 80, 84] to perform tasks through iterative reasoning, action, and interaction with external environments, rather than merely generating responses [46, 4, 78]. Among these environments, command-line interfaces (CLIs) have become one of the most general ways for language models to interact with external systems, use tools, access files, and execute code. As a result, building more capable agentic models requires stronger CLI capabilities.

In this work, we release IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities across a wide range of general and coding tasks, with strengths in software engineering, general-purpose task execution, long-horizon reasoning and execution, and cybersecurity. We also optimize IQuest-Q1 for real-world CLI use, with reliable tool use and robust performance across different agent harnesses.

Methods.

IQuest-Q1 is trained through a multi-stage pipeline (see Figure 2) to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities. General pre-training combines Stable SplitNorm [94, 68], Muon [35], and μ\muP parameterization [75] with a two-stage curriculum that increases the coding-data mixture in the second stage. This design improves scaling efficiency while maintaining a wide stability margin between safe and optimal learning rates. Mid-training then expands the data mixture across domains and formats while progressively extending the context. Post-training (shown in Figure 6) builds diverse CLI [46, 36] capabilities through synthesized tasks executed in production environments. Specifically, SFT establishes basic CLI interaction, while RL enhances capabilities through task-level feedback and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates complementary model capabilities from diverse frozen experts into a unified model. Model merging further combines complementary capabilities from expert models trained for different CLIs, while mitigating conflicts among their parameter updates.

Results.

Figure 1 shows the results of IQuest-Q1 on 8 agentic and reasoning benchmarks, highlighting three aspects of its capabilities: (1) Advancing coding capability. IQuest-Q1 demonstrates coding capabilities across benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1, CyberGym, and NL2Repo. (2) Broad general agentic and reasoning capability. Beyond coding, IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on general agentic and reasoning benchmarks, including JobBench, Agents’ Last Exam, and Humanity’s Last Exam. (3) Optimized CLI interaction experience. On our internal IQuest-CLIBench, IQuest-Q1 manifests user-facing CLI interaction capabilities on interactive task.

Beyond benchmark performance, IQuest-Q1 participates in an iterative model-development process built on our internal infrastructure, contributing to the development of its own successors under human supervision. This human-on-the-loop process provides a practical pathway towards recursive self-improvement, allowing model-generated improvements to accelerate subsequent model iterations.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    IQuest-Q1: an open-weight agentic model optimized for CLI capability. IQuest-Q1 is a sparse MoE model with 320B total parameters, of which 15B are activated per token, combining substantial general-purpose, coding-agent, and CLI interaction capabilities. We release its model weights to support further research and development in the community.

  • •

    CLI-centric training pipeline. We build the training pipeline around CLI-based agentic interaction. Pre-training progressively develops the capabilities required for downstream interaction through staged data mixtures. Post-training specializes these capabilities through task and environment synthesis, multi-scaffold RL, and MOPD to consolidate multiple models into a unified model.

  • •

    Model development with human-on-the-loop RSI. We incorporate IQuest-Q1 into our iterative model-development process, allowing it to evaluate its capabilities and suggest potential improvements through a unified infrastructure interface under human supervision. This process enables continuous model improvement while shortening the overall development cycle.

2 Model Architecture

2.1 Overall Architecture

IQuest-Q1 builds on the Transformer architecture [66] with sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers [17] and hybrid sliding-window attention (see Figure 3). The attention stack interleaves Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) [3] and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) [26]. Within each attention module, a query-aware sink token [1] provides an adaptive destination for excess attention mass. Query–key normalization (QKNorm) stabilizes attention by controlling query and key scales [21], and QKNorm Clip is additionally applied to prevent excessively large affine parameters. Partial RoPE applies rotary position embeddings [57] to only a subset of the dimensions in each attention head. On the feed-forward side, the first Transformer layer replaces sparse MoE routing with a dense MLP to mitigate expert load imbalance in the earliest layer of the model. To improve scaling effectiveness, IQuest-Q1 adopts Stable SplitNorm to increase effective depth [10, 52]. For efficient and stable scaling, we combine the Muon optimizer [35] with μ\muP parameterization [75], supporting efficient optimization and learning-rate transfer across model sizes.

Stable SplitNorm.

Traditional Pre-Norm [72] may underutilize the depth of the model. As the unnormalized residual stream accumulates across layers, its variance can grow with depth, reducing the relative contribution of later residual updates [58]. Motivated by these observations, IQuest-Q1 adopts a hybrid normalization design introduced in prior work [94, 68]. We refer to this design as SplitNorm, which splits the normalization strategy across Transformer sublayers: the residual stream entering the attention sublayer is normalized, whereas the residual stream entering the feed-forward network (FFN) is kept unnormalized. This design combines the stability benefits of Pre-Norm with the stronger depth utilization associated with Post-Norm, mitigating the underutilization of deeper layers in Pre-Norm architectures. Given an input xx, the SplitNorm block used here is formulated using RMSNorm [91] as:

z=RMSNorm⁡(x),h=z+Attention⁡(z),y=h+FFN⁡(RMSNorm⁡(h)).z=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x),\qquad h=z+\mathrm{Attention}(z),\qquad y=h+\mathrm{FFN}\bigl(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(h)\bigr). (1)

where xx denotes the input hidden state, zz denotes the RMSNorm-normalized input, hh is the intermediate representation after the attention block with a residual connection, and yy is the output after the FFN block with another residual connection.

This hybrid design combines normalized attention states with an identity residual path around the FFN. However, directly scaling this formulation to large models can lead to unstable optimization. To address this issue, IQuest-Q1 further introduces two modifications. First, an RMSNorm is applied to the attention output to prevent activation explosion, such that the attention update in Equation 1 becomes h=z+RMSNorm⁡(Attention⁡(z))h=z+\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{Attention}(z)). Second, a SandwichNorm structure [16], implemented with RMSNorm, is used for the first layer to stabilize the model input at the beginning of the residual stream.

μ\muP: Transfer Across Width and Depth.

IQuest-Q1 adopts μ\muP parameterization [75] for width-wise learning-rate transfer. Depth-wise transfer depends on additional parameterization choices, as studied in Depth-μ\muP [76] and CompleteP [14]. Under our adopted parameterization, empirical validation demonstrates hyper-parameter transfer across models spanning a 4×4\times range in width and a 4×4\times range in depth. Instead of tuning the learning rate directly at the target scale, we perform the search on a small proxy model with a hidden width of 896896 and 1818 layers. The learning rate selected on this proxy is then transferred zero-shot to the target model under the adopted parameterization, without additional learning-rate tuning at the target scale. We provide detailed μ\muP scaling factors in Table 3 in the appendix.

Recursive Multi-token Prediction.

To improve backbone learning through additional future-token supervision, we incorporate two multi-token prediction (MTP) [18, 11] layers from the start of pre-training. After completing the training pipeline, we adapt the first layer into a recursive drafter for speculative decoding and discard the second layer in a dedicated training stage. As in EAGLE-3 [33], we extend the speculation horizon with a fixed parameter budget by reusing the same MTP layer across seven drafting steps [8, 90]. In each drafting step, the output hidden state and generated token are fed back into the same MTP layer to produce subsequent predictions. We also replace its attention with SWA using a smaller window, which bounds the per-step attention cost as the context grows. Details can be found in Figure 11 in the appendix.

Scaling efficiency.

To evaluate scaling efficiency, we conduct a controlled comparison between IQuest-Q1 and a representative Qwen3-MoE-style design [74] following the Qwen3-30B-A3B configuration, using identical training data. As shown in 4(a), IQuest-Q1 consistently achieves lower training cross-entropy loss at a given training FLOPs budget. 2.3 Infrastructure

Data Packing.

Sequence packing reduces padding overhead in language-model training [29]. To improve effective token throughput at a fixed sequence length and global batch size, we apply best-fit packing to the globally shuffled data stream using a bounded look-ahead window. The window contains up to 2​B​S2BS tokens, where BB denotes the global batch size and SS the sequence length. Samples left unpacked in the current window are carried over and prioritized in the next iteration, preventing them from being indefinitely delayed by subsequent packing decisions. Long-context training amplifies compute imbalance arising from document-length variation. Packed sequences are therefore reordered across data-parallel replicas to balance computation at micro-batch granularity.

Sink Attention and Context Parallelism.

Context parallelism uses ring-based K/V exchange for full attention [34], while sliding-window attention exchanges only the required halo and overlaps these exchanges with computation in both the forward and backward passes. During halo exchange, each rank computes attention over its local K/V, producing outputs for interior queries and partial outputs with associated Log-Sum-Exp (LSE) statistics for boundary queries. Once the halo arrives, the rank computes the complementary contributions for boundary queries and combines the local and halo partial outputs through LSE-based renormalization. This allows boundary queries to make progress before remote K/V becomes available while preserving sliding-window attention semantics. We illustrate the halo exchange schedule and partial output merging in Figure 10 in the appendix. Both full and sliding-window attention execution paths fuse learnable sink contributions into attention computation to reduce memory traffic.

Correctness Validation.

To reduce silent errors introduced by model and training changes during RSI, the agent mines semantic invariants from the model’s training setup. These invariants are converted into checks that run during distributed training to detect deviations from single-machine semantics and violations of predefined correctness constraints.

3 Pre-Training

3.1 Pre-Training Data

We construct a high-quality, multilingual pre-training corpus spanning diverse domains, drawing from web pages, public GitHub code, books, academic papers, news, and domain-specific materials. For the code, we preserve diversity across programming languages, modalities, and task granularities, dimensions emphasized by prior work on multilingual code generation, multi-granularity evaluation, and repository-level executable completion [15, 13, 28, 9, 73, 79]. Our unified data processing pipeline includes cleaning, quality filtering, exact deduplication, and fuzzy deduplication to reduce noise and redundancy while preserving diversity.

General pre-training proceeds in two stages with a progressively adjusted data mixture. Stage 1 establishes foundational language capabilities and general knowledge through diverse corpora, maximizing unique token counts across multiple domains. Stage 2 gradually increases the proportion of code and STEM data to strengthen programming, mathematical, and scientific problem-solving capabilities. Specifically, we design a four-phase pipeline increasing code data percentage from 40% to 70%.

Mid-training then combines high-quality natural corpora [38], QA pairs [2, 92, 88, 82], and agentic trajectories [45] to prepare the model for downstream reasoning and agentic tasks. Across pre-training and mid-training, the model is trained on a total of 29T tokens.

Model Hyper-Parameters.

As summarized in Table 1, IQuest-Q1 has 8888 Transformer layers and a hidden dimension of 3,0723{,}072. Attention uses 4848 query heads and 88 key–value heads, each with a dimension of 128128. The first two and last two layers use full attention (FA) to capture global information and improve training stability, while the intermediate layers repeat three SWA layers followed by one FA layer, yielding a 3:13{:}1 local-to-global ratio within each repeating block. The SWA uses a window size of 4,0964{,}096. Partial RoPE is applied to 3232 dimensions of each attention head, with RoPE bases of 10,00010{,}000 and 1,000,0001{,}000{,}000 for SWA and FA, respectively. Query-Aware Sink Attention is enabled in all attention layers. The first Transformer layer uses a dense FFN with an intermediate dimension of 12,28812{,}288, while the remaining layers use sparse MoE FFNs. Each MoE layer contains 256256 routed experts, with 88 experts activated per token and an intermediate dimension of 1,5361{,}536 for each expert. Both dense and expert FFNs adopt SwiGLU. The vocabulary size is 160,000160{,}000, with untied input embeddings and output weights. During pre-training, IQuest-Q1 adopts two Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers to improve the performance of the backbone model. Each prediction order uses an embedding dimension of 128128 and 88 attention heads, and the MTP loss is weighted by 0.30.3.

Training Hyper-Parameters.

We employ Muon [35] for all parameters except token embeddings, the language modeling head, normalization parameters, and MoE routers, which are optimized with Adam. For Adam, we set β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95, and ϵ=10−15\epsilon=10^{-15}. For Muon, we set the momentum to 0.950.95. For an m×nm\times n weight matrix, we scale the orthogonalized update by 0.2​max⁡(m,n)0.2\sqrt{\max(m,n)}, combining spectral scaling with an additional factor of 0.20.2 to align the update RMS with that of Adam-style updates [35]. We apply weight decay with a coefficient of 0.10.1 to all parameters except layer normalization parameters, which are exempt from weight decay. We additionally apply QKNorm Clip, capping the affine parameters of QKNorm at 1010. We adopt a warmup-stable-decay learning rate schedule. The learning rate is warmed up to 6×10−46\times 10^{-4} and held constant for the remainder of Stage 1, then decays to 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} by the end of Stage 2 and to 6×10−56\times 10^{-5} by the end of mid-training.

3.3 Mid-Training and Long-Context Extension

3.3.1 Training Curriculum

Mid-training bridges broad pre-training and specialized agent post-training through a curriculum that combines a diverse data mixture, selective token-level supervision, and progressive context extension.

Data Organization.

The mid-training mixture comprises three principal categories: high-quality natural corpora, QA pairs, and agentic trajectories. We organize training data using a chat template adapted for mid-training, retaining a selected subset of special tokens, including those associated with reasoning and tool calls.

Token-Level Loss Masking.

We specify loss masks directly for individual tokens, independently of the role-specific special tokens used to determine supervision in a typical post-training setup. This decouples data formatting from loss computation and allows supervision to be tailored to selected spans within each training example, with finer control than masking entire conversational roles.

Progressive Context Extension.

We extend the maximum training context lengths through 32K, 128K, and 512K tokens, using variable-length sequence packing throughout. The global-attention RoPE base increases from 500,000500,000 at 32K to 1,000,0001,000,000 in the subsequent phases; the hybrid attention pattern, 4,0964,096 sliding window, and SWA RoPE base of 10,00010,000 remain fixed.

Optimization across Phases.

The mid-training learning rate follows a single cosine decay across all three context-length phases, with no additional warmup. At phase transitions, we transfer model weights and reinitialize the optimizer state while preserving the learning-rate schedule’s progress.

3.3.2 Agentic Data Construction Guided by Trajectories

Agentic mid-training requires large and diverse trajectory corpora, but suitable trajectories are scarce and concentrated in a limited set of tasks and environments. To expand coverage while preserving realistic interaction patterns, we use selected trajectories as behavioral anchors and pre-training documents to broaden technical and task coverage.

Using these sources, we construct executable, containerized instances from compatible code repositories, following prior work on tasks derived from repositories and trajectory generation at scale [85, 71]. This process yields more than one million instances. We roll out an agent on each instance and retain valid and complete trajectories for mid-training.

3.4 Evaluation

We evaluate pre-training and mid-training using two complementary types of evaluations. First, we compute bits-per-byte (BPB) on held-out agent trajectories. Lower BPB indicates that the model assigns higher likelihood to behaviors observed in competent agent trajectories, providing a generation-free measure of how well the model captures the trajectory distribution. This metric can provide a fine-grained training signal that complements downstream task-level evaluations.

We further decompose long-horizon agent behavior into atomic abilities and evaluate how reliably the model performs each ability. This fine-grained evaluation helps identify specific capability gaps and informs data selection and curriculum design. Together, these two evaluation paradigms provide complementary signals for tracking and improving agentic capabilities during pre-training and mid-training.

4 Post-Training

4.1 Large-Scale and Diverse Task Synthesis

We organize the task synthesis framework into three settings: general, reasoning, and coding. Each setting uses diverse data sources and a domain-specific pipeline to generate tasks at scale.

General Agent.

We collect APIs and MCP servers from RapidAPI11 1 https://rapidapi.com and Smithery22 2 https://smithery.ai, public skills from the web, and workspace files for task synthesis. Guided by the Standard Occupational Classification [65], we cover a broad range of occupations and synthesize high-coverage environments and tasks, which are iteratively refined through a solve-then-refine loop.

Reasoning Agent.

We synthesize tasks through a document-grounded pipeline that jointly controls concept coverage, material quality, and task difficulty. The pipeline first expands a broad concept inventory into fine-grained scientific topics, then retrieves and curates documents for each topic, filters the documents before synthesis, and finally converts the retained materials into tasks with reference answers. By covering high-value knowledge through the document collection, the pipeline promotes corresponding coverage in the synthesized prompts.

Coding Agent.

We construct executable environments from GitHub repositories and industrial data [27, 48, 85, 12, 83, 81, 77] using multiple versions of coding-agent harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex, with our model driving environment construction and skills supporting setup. Task queries draw on PRs and issues, repository knowledge graphs and documentation, and reusable patterns extracted from cleaned, de-identified usage logs. Skills capture task structure and common failure modes to guide instance synthesis. Verifiers combine agent-written tests, adapted repository tests, and checks derived from documented behavior. For offline instances, external dependencies are replaced by local fixtures or mocks. An agent-judge loop checks executability, leakage, and consistency among instructions, reference solutions, environments, and verifiers, repairing defective instances and rejecting weak assertions. Reference solutions must pass while no-op solutions must fail. Rubric-based trajectory review further filters cheating and low-quality execution beyond binary success. Repeated agent runs estimate difficulty, and overly easy instances are enriched with additional skills or constraints before revalidation; valid instances exposing model failures are retained.

An overview of coding-agent task instances is shown in Figure 5. We construct instances through two complementary modes: building new environments from raw sources and updating verified environments through re-tasking, rewriting, fault injection, evolution, hardening and repair, and selective re-rolling. The resulting library covers software engineering, interactive and multimodal tasks, cybersecurity, and skill-grounded professional work, with domain-specific runtimes and verifiers.

4.2 Environment Integrity and Reward Hacking Mitigation

Agentic training environments are vulnerable to reward hacking, where models exploit leaked solutions or weaknesses in task verifiers instead of solving the intended tasks. Such behavior can contaminate SFT data and introduce misleading reward signals during RL. To prevent this, we apply three layers of protection: environment preparation, execution-time checks, and trajectory auditing.

Environment Preparation.

Before collecting trajectories, we prepare task environments to prevent solution leakage. Depending on the task, we clean Git history, remove files that could reveal existing solutions, or create fresh environments containing only the required materials. We also isolate task environments to prevent unintended access to hidden evaluation data or resources from other tasks.

Execution-Time Checks.

During rollouts, we restrict access to external resources and sensitive task files. Depending on the environment, we enforce network restrictions or intercept tool calls before execution. We develop blocking rules from observed hacking behaviors to prevent agents from retrieving existing solutions, upstream code, or hidden evaluation materials. These checks preserve access to legitimate dependencies and task resources. Blocked operations return explicit feedback, allowing agents to continue without the prohibited access.

Trajectory Auditing.

We further audit collected trajectories using rule-based checks and rubric-guided LLM judgments. The audits examine executed commands, tool outputs, and submitted solutions to identify behaviors such as retrieving leaked fixes, accessing hidden tests, or modifying evaluation scripts. Confirmed hacking trajectories are excluded from training, while suspicious cases can be flagged for further review. We also use detected cases to refine our environment restrictions and blocking rules.

Task-Specific Safeguards.

We adapt these safeguards to the needs of each task. For SWE-like tasks, we keep only the Git history up to the base commit and use hooks in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode to block attempts to retrieve existing solutions. For Terminal-Bench, we remove Git history when it is not needed and check commands before execution when it must be preserved. ProgramBench takes a different approach, building fresh containers with only the compiled oracle and task documentation, without exposing the original repository.

4.3 Supervised Fine-Tuning

As shown in Figure 6, we initialize supervised fine-tuning (SFT) from the mid-trained checkpoint to prepare the policy for reinforcement learning. We optimize the autoregressive cross-entropy loss on assistant responses, including tool-call tokens, while masking user instructions and tool observations from the loss. SFT proceeds in two stages (240B+ tokens in Stage 1 and 50B+ tokens in Stage 2), with initial learning rates of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} and 1.5×10−51.5\times 10^{-5}, respectively, and cosine learning-rate decay within each stage. Multiple samples are packed into each sequence, with attention masking to prevent cross-sample attention.

4.4 Environment-Centered Reinforcement Learning

We outline an RL design that targets verifiable task completion while accounting for user constraints and execution cost. It draws on configurable-harness training in Kimi K3 [61] and domain-specialized Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) in DeepSeek-V4 [12].

Multi-harness, Multi-version Episodes.

To improve the model’s performance across different agent harnesses and versions, we train a shared policy on trajectories collected from diverse harness configurations, including Claude Code, Codex, and their different versions. Each episode specifies a task domain, harness and its version, environment, and evaluator. During training, the policy interacts with different harnesses, observing public instructions, tools, and execution feedback while reference solutions and hidden checks remain isolated. GRPO compares repeated rollouts of the same task under a fixed harness and evaluator version. Sampling balances domain–harness combinations and retains regression cases.

Rewards and Failure Attribution.

Independent verifiers determine terminal correctness. For long trajectories, auxiliary segment-level rewards are restricted to measurable progress, while penalties address unnecessary computation, constraint violations, and reward hacking. Model-generated diagnoses require evidence from execution records before contributing to these signals. Failures are attributed before optimization: policy-caused errors supply learning signals, environment or harness faults unrelated to policy behavior are masked, and evaluator faults block sample consumption. Token-level updates use recorded rollout probabilities through the existing Token-In, Token-Out (TITO) pipeline. The resulting specialized policies can subsequently be consolidated through MOPD.

As shown in Figure 6, starting from SFT Stage 1, we interleave training with residual model merging across stages and within expert branches, ultimately incorporating expert and MOPD checkpoints into IQuest-Q1. 4.7 Post-Training Infrastructure

Multi-harness and Multi-version Agent Runtime.

A single policy can be trained on trajectories from multiple harnesses and versions within one run. Each training instance specifies its scaffold, task environment, and verifier. The runtime executes the corresponding configuration and verifies the task in an isolated sandbox while preserving tool orchestration, context management, and interaction flow. We map different API protocols to a unified policy interface to reduce the difficulty of downstream integrations.

Rollout-training Consistency.

We implement an end-to-end TITO path at the model-serving boundary. Specifically, we apply a session-level prefix tree to retain token histories shared across turns and branches. A request then combines its environment observations with a recorded token prefix. The corresponding response is returned in the structured format expected by the scaffold. Finally, we retain trajectories paired with rewards and token-level masks from the tree at the end of the sequence.

Asynchronous Distillation and Teacher Execution.

We implement MOPD in a fully asynchronous training system. We apply periodic synchronization of student parameters and explicit control of sample staleness, limiting the policy lag introduced by asynchronous execution. We execute teacher forward passes with the training engine on trajectories generated online by the student, producing token-level teacher log probabilities. We use the same execution path for teacher evaluation and student log-probability computation to reduce discrepancies caused by the training engine.

This framework supports independently configured teachers through a common scheduling interface. Teachers reuse the same execution resources through weight switching. We store teacher weights in distributed storage and load them on demand, with only the shards required by the active teacher placed in GPU memory. Weights of the next teacher are prefetched during the current forward pass with overlapping computation. This design supports additional teachers without a proportional increase in resident GPU replicas.

Coding and Software Engineering.

IQuest-Q1 demonstrates a broad range of repository-level coding capabilities, including bug fixing and feature addition, achieving scores of 57.5 on SWE-Bench Pro and 64.6 on DeepSWE v1.1. It also handles repository generation from natural language across NL2Repo-Bench (63.0) and PaperBench (86.0), covering general programming and research code reproduction. General Capabilities.

IQuest-Q1 scores 75.0 on Toolathlon-Verified, 52.7 on AutomationBench, and 77.1 on Claw-Eval, reflecting its capabilities in tool use and multi-step task execution. 6 Capabilities with CLI Agents

6.1 Interactive Frontend Generation

IQuest-Q1 generates diverse interactive frontend applications from user queries, combining visual design, scene construction, and interaction logic in browser-runnable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. These tasks showcase its CLI coding capabilities by turning implementations into interactive artifacts.

We provide examples (see Figure 7) from domains including games, creative tools, and scientific visualization. For example, the underwater sandbox combines an explorable world with building and mining, while the sunset racing game couples vehicle control with camera movement and race-state feedback. The garden editor links flower parameters and planting actions to a 3D scene. Together, they suggest how IQuest-Q1 coordinates rendering, user input, and application state to create interactive web experiences with distinct visual styles.

6.2 Iterative Development under Human Supervision

We illustrate a model development iteration in which an agent built on IQuest-Q1 identifies a capability gap, implements a solution, and evaluates the model under human supervision and intervention. The iteration targets adaptation to different scaffolds and tool-call schemas. While the model handles familiar schemas well, it can fail on unfamiliar ones, producing 35 tool-call errors in one long-horizon task due to mismatched tool names and parameters.

Trace Tool-call Failures and Identify Data Inconsistencies. The agent traces the failures across 6,054 tool calls and finds that the training data is heavily biased toward a single tool-call schema, with some records containing mismatches between tool definitions and call parameters due to preprocessing. It proposes cleaning these inconsistent records and augmenting the training data with diverse tool-call schemas. Human experts review the diagnosis and proposed intervention before approving the training run.

Implement Mixed-schema Data Augmentation and Model Training. The agent implements the data cleaning and augmentation pipeline and prepares the experiment configuration. The training run uses 2.35B tokens and 938.7 GPU hours. The resulting model checkpoint is evaluated on held-out schemas and familiar schemas, while checking for performance regressions.

This iteration demonstrates the potential of iterative model development with IQuest-Q1, while also highlighting the importance of human supervision. The agent drives failure analysis, intervention design, implementation, and evaluation, with human experts reviewing key decisions and controlling costly experiments and changes carried forward to subsequent iterations.

6.3 Cyber Security

Beyond general software engineering tasks, we further evaluate IQuest-Q1 on defensive cybersecurity tasks, where understanding and validating vulnerabilities are essential for improving software security. IQuest-Q1 achieves a score of 84.5 on CyberGym [67], a benchmark that evaluates the ability to reproduce and validate real-world vulnerabilities in large open-source codebases, providing evidence to support vulnerability diagnosis and remediation.

We further assess the practical utility of these capabilities in real-world security workflows. During a three-day deployment, human cyber security experts, assisted by IQuest-Q1, produced 30 vulnerability reports. All reports were independently validated by fellow security experts, and findings affecting open-source projects were responsibly disclosed to their respective maintainers. The participating experts reported that IQuest-Q1 provided substantial support for their defensive security work, particularly in understanding and validating security issues.

Limitations

  • •

    Text-only input. IQuest-Q1 has no native image, audio, or video input capability.

  • •

    Output reliability. Generated explanations and code may be incorrect. Code changes should be reviewed or verified with task-appropriate tests.

  • •

    Tool integration. Tool calls use the IQuest-specific format in the chat template. Structured tool execution and reasoning extraction require compatible serving parsers and an agent harness.

  • •

    Challenges in Real-World CLI Tasks. Real-world CLI tasks often require iterative debugging and verification. IQuest-Q1 may overlook constraints, repeat failed attempts, or leave issues unresolved, necessitating human review and supervision.

  • •

    Ongoing development. IQuest-Q1 still has limitations in its capabilities and reliability, and we will continue to advance its capabilities. Furthermore, we release the model weights, deployment configurations, and agent-integration instructions to facilitate further research and continued development in the community.

Conclusion

We present IQuest-Q1, an open-source agentic foundation model with broad CLI capabilities. We train IQuest-Q1 through a multi-stage pipeline to progressively develop general knowledge, long-context capabilities, and agentic CLI capabilities. IQuest-Q1 demonstrates capabilities on coding, general agentic tasks, and reasoning-heavy tasks. Furthermore, IQuest-Q1 participates in our internal iterative model-development loop, providing a foundation for continuing model development.

Appendix A Pre-Training

Safe learning rate.

We perform a grid search over learning rates and classify the resulting training-loss trajectories as stable, warning, or collapsed, as illustrated in Figure 8. Stable runs show consistently decreasing loss; warning runs exhibit a transient rebound before recovering, while collapsed runs rebound and remain at high loss. We define the safe learning rate, ηsafe\eta_{\mathrm{safe}}, as the largest tested learning rate classified as stable.

μ\muP scaling factors.

Table 3 summarizes the width- and depth-dependent scaling rules used to train IQuest-Q1. Following CompleteP [14], we apply an output scaling factor of L−1/2L^{-1/2} to both the attention and FFN branches. For the attention branch, this factor is incorporated into the output RMSNorm. For the FFN branch, it is applied directly to the branch output.

As shown in Figure 9, these scaling rules enable consistent transfer of the optimal learning rate across models with different widths and depths.

Recursive Multi-token Prediction.

Figure 11 illustrates the workflow of recursive multi-token prediction. We adopt the MTP architecture of DeepSeek-V3 [11], which concatenates a hidden representation with a token embedding to form the input to the MTP block. At the first drafting step, the hidden representation comes from the final layer of the backbone model. At each subsequent step, we concatenate the previous step’s output hidden representation with the embedding of the token predicted at that step and feed the result back into the same MTP block, enabling recursive draft generation with shared parameters.
